title: Otero County Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Otero County wells have a 40-foot median depth. Review local yields, water levels, permit history and modeled finished-well costs of $7,400-$14,200.
h1: What to Expect from a Well in Otero County
intro_html:
Shallow wells dominate Otero County's records, but the deeper end of the inventory is a different drilling job entirely. The median depth is 40 feet, while 10% reach 600 feet or more. Before pricing a property near Rocky Ford, Swink or La Junta, find out which kind of well serves the surrounding lots.

Colorado DWR records contain 3,335 permitted wells countywide, with 2,318 recorded as constructed. These records mix household, stock, irrigation and monitoring uses. They are a useful starting point for a purchase or drilling bid, not a promise of water on a particular parcel.

sections.heading: A Shallow Median, but a Deep Tail in Otero County
sections.html:
Of the 2,271 wells reporting depth, the middle half fall between 31 and 62 feet. With 78% under 100 feet, a shallow drilling allowance can make sense where nearby construction logs support it. It should not become a fixed assumption in a land purchase.

The 90th-percentile depth is 590 feet, and the deepest recorded well reaches 1,990 feet. Ground here includes alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. Permits name Dakota for 92 wells and Alluvial for 40, but 3,098 carry an unnamed / fractured-bedrock aquifer label. That broad label does not establish the geology beneath your lot. Ask the driller to identify the likely water-bearing material and price deeper drilling separately.

sections.heading: Why the 25 gpm Median Needs a Use Check
sections.html:
The reported median pump yield is 25.0 gpm, with a middle half of 12.0-240.0 gpm. That wide spread needs context: only 272 wells report yield, and the county inventory includes 25% irrigation and 25% stock uses alongside 38% domestic/household use. The county median is not a household-well performance guarantee.

Among reported yields, 70% are at least 15 gpm, 29% are in the 5-15 gpm band, and 1% are in the 1-5 gpm band. None report under 1 gpm. That is encouraging, but it does not rule out low production or unsuccessful drilling. For a purchase, request a sustained pumping and recovery test rather than relying only on the permit's yield entry.

sections.heading: Otero's Water-Level Records Do Not Show a Falling Table
sections.html:
Static water level is the depth to resting water, not the bottom of the well. Otero County's median is 20 feet below ground, and the middle half spans 12-35 feet. Only 84 wells report this measurement, so the picture is much thinner than the depth inventory.

Decade medians are 28 feet in the 1950s, 25 feet in the 2010s and 18 feet in the 2020s. Those measurements become shallower, not deeper; they do not suggest a dropping water table in this dataset. They also are not repeated measurements of the same wells. Have the property's current static level and pumping drawdown checked before treating these county figures as evidence of dependable supply.

sections.heading: The Permit History Behind Today's Well Inventory
sections.html:
Otero County's permit record includes 314 permits from the 1950s, followed by larger totals of 460 in the 1990s and 480 in the 2000s. The 2010s account for 262, and the 2020s for 130, with the newest permit year listed as 2025. The latest decade is incomplete, and permit issuance is not the same as completed drilling.

Leading driller entries include Crandall, H A with 211 records and Broce Drilling (Broce, Frank R.) with 140. Another prominent entry, Authorized (Pe, Pg), accounts for 189; treat that as a record label rather than an identified drilling business. These are historical counts, not confirmation that a contractor is currently available. Check current licensing and local experience when seeking bids.

sections.heading: Budgeting a New Well Near Swink or Rocky Ford
sections.html:
The Otero County cost model uses $35-$55 per foot for drilling in alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the 40-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $1,400-$2,200. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $7,400-$14,200.

The hole price is not the working-water-system price. Ask for an itemized scope covering casing, grout, development, pump equipment and the route to the house. The 31-62-foot middle depth range gives a useful shallow-well starting point, but a Dakota or other deeper target needs its own estimate. Get written terms for added depth and unsuccessful drilling before equipment arrives.

sections.heading: Environmental Flags and Site Conditions to Investigate
sections.html:
The mapped environmental inventory within about 10 miles includes 22 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 16 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites and 10 historic mine features. These are screening flags, not proof that a particular Otero County well is contaminated. A sampling location is not necessarily a confirmed contamination source.

Review the site records in relation to the parcel and discuss appropriate laboratory testing with the local health authority. Inspect the wellhead, casing condition and surface drainage, especially where runoff could reach the well. Low-yield risk still needs testing despite the reported 0% share under 1 gpm. For a new build, coordinate the well, septic system, replacement septic area and building footprint before grading or choosing the final house location.

sections.heading: Before Closing on Land Around La Junta or Fowler
sections.html:
Start with the actual parcel, not the county median. Around La Junta Gardens, North La Junta, Fowler, Manzanola or Cheraw, compare nearby wells for depth, construction details, reported yield and permitted use. A close neighbor's log is more useful for a preliminary bid than a countywide average, though it still cannot guarantee the same result.

Match the property's DWR permit to the existing well and confirm that its allowed uses fit your plans. Household permission does not automatically authorize irrigation or other outdoor uses. A new or expanded supply may face augmentation requirements in an over-appropriated basin. Make satisfactory permit review, water testing and a workable well-and-septic layout part of purchase due diligence.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Otero County, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded depth is 40 feet, and the middle half runs 31-62 feet. Most are shallow: 78% are under 100 feet. But 10% reach 600 feet or more. Review neighboring construction logs before budgeting, because the county's shallow median does not describe every aquifer or parcel.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Otero County?
faq.a: The local model uses $35-$55 per foot. At the 40-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $1,400-$2,200, while a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $7,400-$14,200. Ask for a parcel-specific estimate and written pricing for additional depth; these figures are not a fixed bid.

faq.q: How much water do Otero County wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 272 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 25.0 gpm and the middle half is 12.0-240.0 gpm. The records mix household, stock and irrigation wells, so that range is not a residential design target. Have an existing well tested for sustained output and recovery before buying.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Otero County?
faq.a: Safety has to be established for the individual well through testing. The mapped inventory within about 10 miles includes 22 PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 16 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites, but proximity alone does not establish contamination. Review nearby site information, inspect the well's sanitary condition and arrange laboratory testing appropriate to the property.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Otero County?
faq.a: The available decade medians do not show a dropping table: depth to water was 28 feet in the 1950s, 25 feet in the 2010s and 18 feet in the 2020s. Those are shallower readings, but only 84 wells report static levels. Different wells and measurement conditions prevent treating this as a parcel-level trend.
